headline: Tom Kim's gold medal just cost the army 18 months.
summary: South Korean golfer Tom Kim, 24, shot a six-under 64 in Japan to win the Asian Games by three strokes. South Korean men owe 18 to 21 months of military service before they turn 28. An Asian Games gold or any Olympic medal cuts that to basic training, under a month. Kim flew in from the Presidents Cup in the US on six hours of sleep.

cover_question.q: Should a medal skip the army?

cover_answer: South Korea says yes. His 18 months is now under one.
table_question: Should being great at one thing get you out of a job everyone does?

5-7.script: A golfer from South Korea named Tom Kim won a gold medal in Japan. In his country every young man has to spend about a year and a half in the army, longer than a whole school year. Win a gold medal and the country says you can do a few weeks instead. When his last putt dropped he let out a roar.
5-7.why: A medal, a long job made short, a roar. Nothing here to worry about.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them the roar and the long job made short. A school year is the anchor, time they have felt pass. Expect "do you have to go in the army?" No. Here nobody has to. There every young man does, and this one earned a shortcut.

8-12.script: Every man in South Korea serves 18 to 21 months in the army before he turns 28. Win gold at the Asian Games, or any Olympic medal, and you do only basic training, under a month. Tom Kim, 24, missed at the Paris Olympics. This time he shot 64 and won by three. A hall pass you earn by beating everyone.
8-12.why: A rule, a miss, a second chance. A hall pass they know.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether they are applied evenly, so the script hands them the rule first: 18 months, one exemption, one way to earn it. Paris is the miss, Japan the second chance, the hall pass the mechanism. Expect "what if he'd come second?" At the Asian Games, second gets nothing. His teammate found that out.

13-17.script: Should a gold medal get you out of the army? South Korea says yes. Tom Kim, 24, won the Asian Games by three shots, and his 18 to 21 months of service becomes basic training, under a month. Second: teammate SH Kim, 28, took silver in the team event. Silver gets nothing. Fair, or exactly the point?
13-17.why: Two Kims, one medal apart. Let them judge the line.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a country may reward the people who win for it, and the line between gold and silver falls on one man with no second chance at 28. The script asks where they would draw it. Expect "isn't that a rule for rich athletes?" Son Heung-min used it too. Ask who it leaves out.

5-7.q: Does Tom Kim have to be a soldier now?
5-7.a: Only for a few weeks of training, not the year and a half. The medal earned him that.

8-12.q: Why does a medal get you out of the army?
8-12.a: South Korea rewards athletes who win for it. Basic training still happens.

8-12.q: What about the players who lost?
8-12.a: The full 18 to 21 months, unless they win an Olympic medal before 28.

13-17.q: Should a medal skip the army?
13-17.a: South Korea thinks winning for the country counts as service. You can argue it either way.
No. Six hours of sleep after flying from the US, then a 64 under pressure.
